# Craftar

> Open-source CLI (TypeScript/Node) that treats an AI-coding harness — rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks, MCP servers — as source in a Git repository (the Forge), composes it per team from reusable ingredients, and emits it in the native format of each AI coder (Claude Code, Kiro, and an AGENTS.md that Codex, Cursor, Warp, Copilot and Kimi read) into every workspace, with a lockfile for drift detection and a per-machine registry of workspaces.

This file is the plain-text companion of the Craftar page (index.html), written for language models and other automated readers. Same content, no layout; diagrams are described in prose — verbatim from the accessible description of each figure — and the two whose topology carries the argument are also given as Mermaid graphs.

## Terminology

- Harness: everything that shapes how coding agents behave in a repository — rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks, MCP servers.
- Forge: one Git repository holding every ingredient, recipe and profile. Versioned; workspaces point at it by local path or by git URL, with an optional branch, tag or full SHA; a remote Forge is read from a per-machine cache. It is never a Git remote of any team repository.
- Ingredient: smallest reusable unit — a rule, agent, command, skill, hook, MCP server, script, steering file or local service. A folder with an `ingredient.yaml` declaring type, targets, inclusion mode and globs. A `service` is aimed at no AI coder: `sync` writes it under `.craftar/`. Project templates are not an ingredient: a profile declares them.
- Recipe: named set of ingredients with parameters. Recipes `extend` others; stack recipes declare a `slot` so two stacks for the same role (e.g. two front-end frameworks) cannot coexist.
- Profile: one team — its recipes, repositories, template feeds, project-management tool, internal platform, and which AI coders that team uses; parameters and section overrides for the whole stack live here.
- Workspace: a local folder (one repo or a folder of repos) with a `craftar.yaml` declaring profile, recipe add/remove (edited by `craftar add recipe` / `remove recipe`) and targets, plus a git-ignored `craftar.local.yaml` for per-developer overrides.
- Target: an AI coder to emit for — `claude-code`, `kiro` and `agents-md` are the targets; Codex, Cursor, Warp, Copilot and Kimi read the emitted `AGENTS.md`. Coverage is a table in the CLI — `craftar targets` prints it, per ingredient type: native, converted or unsupported. Sync skips an ingredient aimed at a target that the table marks unsupported, and warns, naming it — a fallback is planned.
- Lockfile (`craftar.lock`): the Forge's source, requested ref and commit (null when the Forge is not a git repository or has no commits yet), the resolved profile, recipes and targets, and a normalized content hash for every generated file; the lock is rewritten only when its own content changes. The only authority on what Craftar owns in a workspace.
- Registry (`~/.craftar/registry.json`): every workspace a writing `sync` ran in on this machine, with path, profile, Forge, recipes, targets and last sync. `craftar workspaces` lists them with a status computed on the spot; `forget` and `prune` remove entries, and `CRAFTAR_NO_REGISTRY` turns the registry off. `craftar ui` shows them as a local, read-only page on `127.0.0.1`. `craftar ls` stays the view of one workspace's resolved recipes and ingredients.

## Problem statement

Two problems, one root: the harness has no source and no record.

### P1 — One harness, T teams, K AI coders, A agents each, maintained by hand

A harness is a roster of agents (a reviewer per architecture, a docs author, an executor) plus the rules they are bound to, workflow commands, hooks and MCP servers. Across T teams it exists as T copies in K formats (`.claude/`, `.kiro/`, `AGENTS.md`, `.cursor/`), each holding the same A agents. A change costs T × K manual edits, with no record of what was generated from what.

Requires: one source; emission per target; a record per file.

```mermaid
graph LR
  H["harness on the developer's machine · 12 rules · 7 agents · 9 commands · skills · hooks · 4 MCP servers"]
  H -->|copy and translate by hand| A["team A · Claude Code · .claude/ · two months old"]
  H -->|copy and translate by hand| B["team B · Kimi · AGENTS.md · one stale agent"]
  H -->|copy and translate by hand| C["team C · Kiro · .kiro/ · one agent missing"]
  H -->|copy and translate by hand| D["team D · Cursor · .cursor/ · version 3 of 5"]
```

State today (diagram): a single harness — about 12 rules, 7 agents, 9 commands, skills, hooks and 4 MCP servers — exists only as a folder on the developer's machine. It is copied and translated by hand into four team workspaces: team A uses Claude Code, team B uses Kimi via `AGENTS.md`, team C uses Kiro, team D uses Cursor. Because the copies are manual, they diverge: team A's copy is two months old, team B has one stale agent, team C is missing one agent, team D carries version 3 of 5. No edge in this graph is recorded anywhere, so nothing can report which copy is current.

### P2 — One developer, many workspaces, separate remotes

One machine, one workspace per team. Each workspace groups that team's repositories cloned from that team's own Git host; no repository is common to all of them. The harness in each workspace was copied in by hand at a different time. Nothing on the machine records which version each workspace carries, or whether a file in `.claude/` is still the copy or has been edited in place.

Requires: a channel that is no team repository's remote; a lock per workspace; a registry.

State today (diagram): one developer machine holds four workspaces, `workspace-1` to `workspace-4`, one per team. Each workspace contains that team's repositories cloned from that team's own Git remote (four different hosts), so no repository is shared across workspaces. Each workspace also contains a hand-copied `.claude/` harness of unknown version — v3?, v2?, v5?, v4+? — copied at different times or edited in place, with no lockfile. The harness moves from one workspace to the next by hand, one copy at a time, which is how the versions drift apart. The machine has no registry of workspaces, no shared source for the harness, and no way to verify versions.

## Failure modes (observed in earlier generators and hand-synchronised workspaces)

- FM-1 Regeneration deletes hand-written agents and rules. Cause: the generator treats the whole `.claude/` folder as its output.
- FM-2 Every file reports as hand-edited on every run; the team runs permanently on `--force`. Cause: drift guard hashes raw bytes while Git rewrites LF→CRLF on Windows checkout.
- FM-3 A deleted rule keeps loading into sessions. Cause: the generator only writes and never removes outputs of ingredients that left the set.
- FM-4 Second-target mirrors (steering, agent JSON, commands) diverge from their source. Cause: only rules were generated; the rest was kept as manual mirrors.
- FM-5 An architecture rule and its reviewer agent contradict each other. Cause: two files stating the same constraints, edited independently.
- FM-6 A model pin or MCP version breaks in several places at once. Cause: volatile values inlined in multiple files instead of declared once.
- FM-7 A workspace-wide language policy contradicted by many files. Cause: language treated as a property of the workspace instead of each ingredient.
- FM-8 Real tokens in a generated settings file. Cause: generated settings carried values instead of environment-variable references.

FM-1 to FM-5 stem from P1; FM-6 to FM-8 from maintaining P2 by hand.

## Model: source, resolution, emission

Craftar borrows the shape of a build system. Ingredients are source; recipes and profiles compose them; `craftar sync` resolves the composition for one workspace and emits target-specific outputs, recording every output in the lockfile. Generated files are committed to the workspace, so a team that only uses one AI coder never needs Craftar installed.

Layer resolution, weakest to strongest: `base` recipe → stack recipes → team profile → `craftar.yaml` (workspace, committed) → `craftar.local.yaml` (one developer, git-ignored). Same-named ingredients resolve to the strongest layer; stack recipes sharing a `slot` are mutually exclusive; `{{params}}` are substituted from the winning layer. `craftar explain <file>` prints the layer that decided each output.

Pipeline of `craftar sync`:
1. Read `craftar.yaml`; load the Forge (a local path, or a git URL at a branch, tag or full SHA, fetched into a per-machine cache).
2. Resolve layers, exclusive slots and params into the final ingredient set.
3. Emit the open standards: `AGENTS.md` — the always-on rules, then each scoped rule listed at the file a target writes for it, or embedded in full when none does — Agent Skills (`SKILL.md`) and `mcp.json` through the target emitters.
4. Emit tool-specific formats (inclusion modes, subagents, hooks) through Craftar's own emitters and post-processors; delegating further formats to rulesync is planned.
5. Diff against `craftar.lock`; classify each file as new / update / unchanged / adopt / drift / collision / orphan; write, remove orphans, refresh the lock.

Targets in their native format, generated and committed: `claude-code` → `.claude/` and `.mcp.json`; `kiro` → `.kiro/steering` and `.kiro/agents/*.json`; `agents-md` → a root `AGENTS.md`, read by Codex, Cursor, Warp, Copilot and Kimi. Composed files carry a `GENERATED` banner — Kiro steering's is configurable, `AGENTS.md`'s is fixed — while Claude Code text files are emitted verbatim, which is what lets an existing workspace be adopted byte for byte. What Craftar owns is recorded in `craftar.lock`, not in a header; a `generated by craftar from forge@sha` marker on every target is planned.

P1 resolved (diagram): the Forge is one Git repository containing ingredients (rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks, MCP servers, scripts, steering files), recipes (`base`, `backend-*`, `frontend-*`, `aws-local`, `pm-*`) and one profile per team. Running `craftar sync` in a workspace loads the Forge (by path, or by git URL at a ref), resolves layers, emits files for each of the workspace's targets and writes `craftar.lock`. Team A emits to `.claude/` with 7 agents; team B swaps the frontend recipe and has three workspaces, one target each — `.claude/`, `.kiro/` and `AGENTS.md`, which carries the rules only; team C emits `.kiro/` and pins the Forge at tag `v2.3`, which leaves it two commits behind — reporting how far behind is planned; team D sets its targets to agents-md in its local file, so Cursor reads the emitted `AGENTS.md`, which carries the rules only, and has one drifted file. Every edge is generated and recorded in the lock.

P1 resolved — solid edges are generated and recorded in each workspace's lockfile; `status` reads the lock to report drift per workspace and, with a remote Forge, names the Forge commit next to the lock's when it has moved; counting how far behind is planned.

```mermaid
graph LR
  F["Forge · one Git repository · ingredients, recipes, profiles"] --> CR["craftar · reads the Forge at its ref, emits per target"]
  CR --> W1["workspace-1 · .claude/ · craftar.lock 7c1e9a2 · up to date"]
  CR --> W2["workspace-2 · AGENTS.md · craftar.lock 7c1e9a2 · up to date"]
  CR --> W3["workspace-3 · .kiro/ · craftar.lock 5b0d3f1 · outdated, forge moved"]
  CR --> W4["workspace-4 · AGENTS.md · craftar.lock 7c1e9a2 · drift"]
  R1["team 1 Git remote"] -->|git clone| W1
  R2["team 2 Git remote"] -->|git clone| W2
  R3["team 3 Git remote"] -->|git clone| W3
  R4["team 4 Git remote"] -->|git clone| W4
  REG["~/.craftar/registry.json · read by craftar workspaces"] -.-> W1 & W2 & W3 & W4
```

P2 resolved (diagram): same developer machine and same four workspaces as the problem statement, `workspace-1` to `workspace-4`, each still cloning its team's repositories from that team's own remote. Now a fifth repository, the Forge, is referenced by each workspace's `craftar.yaml` and is not a remote of any team repository. Between them sits `craftar` itself: it reads the Forge and emits each workspace's harness, so nothing flows from the Forge to a workspace except through it. Each workspace carries a generated harness with the same base ingredients and a `craftar.lock` naming the Forge commit that produced it (`7c1e9a2` for three of them, `5b0d3f1` for the one synced before the Forge moved). Every writing sync records its workspace in the registry at `~/.craftar/registry.json`, and `craftar workspaces` reports per workspace: up to date, outdated with forge moved, or drift.

## In practice — Forge → Workspace by stack

The layer resolution above is the logical flow — layers resolving into targets. This is the physical mapping: how a real Forge for a given stack becomes actual files in the workspace. Select a stack, then a target to see what `craftar sync` writes today. Every stack lists the same three targets the CLI emits: Claude Code, Kiro and AGENTS.md. In each workspace, `craftar.yaml` is the input the workspace owns and `craftar.lock` is generated.

### dotnet-enterprise — .NET backend teams following Clean Architecture

Forge structure:
- ingredients/rules/: dotnet-clean-architecture, dotnet-clean-code, dotnet-minimal-api, dotnet-entity-framework, dotnet-security
- ingredients/agents/: dotnet-arch-reviewer, dotnet-api-reviewer, dotnet-ef-reviewer, dotnet-security-reviewer
- ingredients/commands/: create-api-endpoint
- recipes/: dotnet-clean-arch.yaml
- profiles/: team-dotnet/

Workspace output (Claude Code target):
- .claude/rules/: dotnet-clean-architecture.md, dotnet-clean-code.md, dotnet-minimal-api.md, dotnet-entity-framework.md, dotnet-security.md
- .claude/agents/: dotnet-arch-reviewer.md, dotnet-api-reviewer.md, dotnet-ef-reviewer.md, dotnet-security-reviewer.md
- .claude/commands/: create-api-endpoint.md
- src/ (client code, untouched)

Workspace output (Kiro target):
- .kiro/steering/: *.md (same rules)
- .kiro/steering/commands/: create-api-endpoint.md
- .kiro/agents/: *.json (agents as JSON)

Workspace output (AGENTS.md target):
- AGENTS.md (always-on rules concatenated, then the scoped rules embedded in full — no other target writes them here)
- One file: the emitter composes the rules only. The four agents and the command have no AGENTS.md expression; the emitter skips them rather than inventing a format, and sync warns once per skipped type, naming each one.

### node-fullstack — Node.js teams using TypeScript

Forge structure:
- ingredients/rules/: node-typescript-strict, node-express-patterns, node-testing-jest, node-eslint-prettier, node-security-headers
- ingredients/agents/: node-arch-reviewer, node-api-reviewer, node-test-reviewer, node-deps-reviewer
- ingredients/commands/: create-express-route
- ingredients/mcp/: npm-audit
- recipes/: node-express-ts.yaml
- profiles/: team-node/

Workspace output (Claude Code target):
- .claude/rules/, .claude/agents/, .claude/commands/
- .mcp.json (npm-audit MCP)

Workspace output (Kiro target):
- .kiro/steering/: *.md, with .kiro/steering/commands/create-express-route.md
- .kiro/agents/: *.json
- .kiro/settings/mcp.json (npm-audit MCP)

Workspace output (AGENTS.md target):
- AGENTS.md (always-on rules concatenated, then the scoped rules embedded in full — no other target writes them here)
- One file: the emitter composes the rules only. The four agents, the command and the npm-audit MCP have no AGENTS.md expression; the emitter skips them rather than inventing a format, and sync warns once per skipped type, naming each one.

### iac-multicloud — Platform teams managing infrastructure as code

Forge structure:
- ingredients/rules/: aws-cloudformation, aws-cdk-typescript, azure-arm-bicep, kubernetes-helm, terraform-modules
- ingredients/agents/: aws-yaml-reviewer, azure-iac-reviewer, k8s-manifest-reviewer, terraform-reviewer
- ingredients/commands/: create-aws-stack, create-helm-chart
- recipes/: iac-aws.yaml, iac-kubernetes.yaml
- profiles/: team-platform/

Workspace output (Claude Code target):
- .claude/rules/: aws-cloudformation.md, aws-cdk-typescript.md, azure-arm-bicep.md, kubernetes-helm.md, terraform-modules.md
- .claude/agents/, .claude/commands/
- infra/ (client IaC, untouched)

Workspace output (Kiro target):
- .kiro/steering/: *.md, with .kiro/steering/commands/: *.md
- .kiro/agents/: *.json

Workspace output (AGENTS.md target):
- AGENTS.md (always-on rules concatenated, then the scoped rules embedded in full — no other target writes them here)
- One file: the emitter composes the rules only. The four agents and the two commands have no AGENTS.md expression; the emitter skips them rather than inventing a format, and sync warns once per skipped type, naming each one.

### What syncs where

Craftar writes the AI coder's own files — `.claude/` plus `.mcp.json` for Claude Code, `.kiro/` for Kiro — and a root `AGENTS.md` for the tools that read the open standard: Codex, Cursor, Warp, Copilot and Kimi consume that file; Craftar writes no tool-agnostic output such as `docs/`. For a workspace whose recipes bring a `service` ingredient, `sync` also writes `.craftar/` — `.craftar/compose.yaml`, `.craftar/.gitattributes` and `.craftar/services/<name>/…` — for no target. Client-owned folders like `src/` or `infra/` are never touched — only paths recorded in `craftar.lock` are ever written or removed. Outside a workspace and a Forge, Craftar writes on its own only under `~/.craftar` (by default): the Forge cache and the registry.

### Growing the Forge — a second client, one base

Importing a second client into an existing Forge keeps every ingredient that already matches and turns the ones that differ into variants named after the profile, so both workspaces still reproduce byte for byte. The `forge` commands then close the gap: `forge variants` lists them nearest first, `forge diff` shows each hunk with a suggested class, and `forge unify` resolves one — keeping the base or the variant, turning the differing value into a parameter the profile carries, or turning a differing block into a section whose content the profile carries. Before and after it writes, `forge unify` plans every workspace registered on this machine that reads the Forge and prints which of each one's files the unification changes; with `--prune-recipes` it also deletes a recipe the unification left identical to its sibling and repoints the profiles that name it — only when every one of those workspaces plans the same files. `craftar forge impact` lists the same workspaces with what each one's next `sync` would do against the Forge as it stands.

Unification (diagram): the Forge already holds `rule/deploy`, whose text reads "use globex-api here". Importing a second client, `acme`, whose copy reads "use acme-api here", keeps the base and adds a variant, `rule/deploy--acme`, that emits under the original name. `craftar forge diff rule/deploy` shows one hunk, `globex-api` against `acme-api`, and suggests the class `value`. `craftar forge unify rule/deploy --profile acme --plan plan.yaml`, with that hunk set to `take: param` and the key `deploy.api`, rewrites the base to "use {{deploy.api}} here", declares `globex-api` as the key's default in the base's `ingredient.yaml`, writes `deploy.api: acme-api` into `profiles/acme/profile.yaml` and removes the variant. Every path it overwrites or deletes must be held by git. Re-importing `acme` afterwards compares its file with the base as sync renders it for `acme`, finds them equal and reuses the base: no variant, no change to the profile.

One rule, two clients. `forge unify` never merges `ingredient.yaml` and refuses when another layer, profile or ingredient already uses the key. Sections ship too — markers placed by hand (each client's content inferred by import) or extracted from a variant by `forge unify` with `take: section`; `forge promote` ships as well — a profile's variant becomes the base, and every other profile that resolved the old base keeps it as a variant of its own. The interactive walk is planned.

## Capabilities (F1–F12; "working" = runs today and is covered by tests; "mvp" = first release; "planned" = designed, not built)

- F1 Forge → workspace sync [working, mvp] (P1, P2): `craftar sync [--dry-run] [--check] [--overwrite-drift]`, `diff [--exit-code]` (what sync would change, an orphan shown as the removal of the whole file, a hand-edited one as a header; with `--exit-code`, exit 1 exactly when `sync --check` would fail), `status` (per file: new, update, unchanged, adopt, drift, collision, orphan, orphan-drift); sync prints what it wrote, removed and skipped, file by file. With a git-URL Forge, `ref` follows a branch or pins a tag or full SHA; sync fetches first and fails when it cannot, so CI never syncs from a stale copy unless it passes `--offline`, which reads the cached copy. `craftar cache prune [--dry-run]` removes the Forge cache entries nothing uses — no registered workspace and not the current one — entries whose first fetch never completed, and trees unused for 14 days; it never touches a workspace, a lock or the registry, and `--dry-run` shows what it would remove. Planned: `--targets`, `update`.
- F2 Multi-target emission [working, mvp] (P1): `craftar import --from claude-code`; Craftar's own emitters for Claude Code, Kiro (byte-identical to a hand-built workspace, including agent JSON and command mirrors) and AGENTS.md; post-processors for gaps (e.g. Kiro agent `resources`). Importing a second client into an existing Forge reuses every ingredient whose render for that profile equals the workspace file, infers declared `{{key}}` values into the profile, and makes the rest variants; `craftar forge variants` (where clients differ, nearest first), `craftar forge diff <type/name>` (hunks, each with a suggested class) and `craftar forge unify <type/name> --profile <p> --plan <file>` (base, variant, param or section) resolve each one back into its base (see Growing the Forge); `craftar forge promote <type/name> --profile <p>` goes the other way — it makes a profile's variant the base and gives the old base back, as a variant of its own, to every other profile that resolved it, gated on git, proved before the first write, never a commit; `craftar forge impact` lists every registered workspace reading this Forge and what its next sync would do; `craftar targets` prints the capability matrix — what each target does with each ingredient type. `craftar import --report <file.md>` also writes a Markdown report of the import: what was created, reused, made a variant or rejected, and the `.kiro/` files that differ from what `sync` would generate — as paths and line counts, never content. `craftar import --prefer-kiro <rule,…>` takes the named rules from `.kiro/steering/<name>.md` instead of `.claude/rules/<name>.md`, for a steering mirror that was edited by hand and is the text to keep; the text is accepted only when it is proved to render back to that steering file's body for Kiro. Rules only: commands, agents and skills are not taken from Kiro. Import reads a Claude rule's `paths:` frontmatter as its scope, so a scoped rule stays scoped — `fileMatch` for Kiro, and a scoped rule in `AGENTS.md` — and keeps that frontmatter verbatim, so `.claude/rules/<name>.md` comes back byte for byte. Planned: rulesync for further tool-specific formats.
- F3 Layers and stack slots [working] (P1): layer resolution, exclusive slots, params, `explain`; `craftar.local.yaml` (git-ignored) overrides the workspace for one developer, its arrays replacing the workspace's; sections — a client-specific block in an ingredient body marked `<!-- craftar:section flavors -->` … `<!-- /craftar:section -->`, whose content is the default and which a profile's `sections` or the workspace's `overrides.sections` replace or empty, with no rendered body holding the markers and `explain` naming the layer each came from; `forge unify` can extract one from a variant (`take: section`); a Forge that uses sections declares `schema: 2` or above, so an older CLI refuses it rather than leak the markers; `craftar recipes` and `craftar ingredients` list the whole Forge read-only, mark what the workspace uses (and, for recipes, why), and `--recipe` shows what choosing one would bring. `craftar add recipe` and `craftar remove recipe` change the workspace's choice in `craftar.yaml` in place — refusing a recipe that would share a slot (unless `--replace`), removing one another recipe still brings in through `extends`, or an edit that would not resolve — and print what the next `sync` would do; they never sync.
- F4 Workspace bootstrap [working] (P2): `craftar init --forge <dir|url> --profile <name>` (with `--targets`, `--add-recipe`, `--remove-recipe`, `--clone`; `--new-profile <name> [--like <profile>]` in place of `--profile`) writes `craftar.yaml` — the Forge, the profile, and the recipe and target choices, given as flags or as answers — only once the workspace resolves and plans, then runs the first `sync`, which registers the workspace; files already on disk are adopted when they equal the plan and otherwise left as they are and reported; an existing `craftar.yaml` is never edited. In a terminal, `craftar init` asks for a `--forge` or a `--profile` it was not given — the Forge last synced on this machine offered, the profile from the Forge's list, then the recipes and targets to keep or adjust — confirms once before anything is written, and ends by printing the same run as flags, for CI; off a terminal a missing flag is refused. When a declared parameter a file the plan writes cites has no value, `craftar.yaml` is still written and the first `sync` is not run. With `--clone` it then clones each repository the profile's `repos` lists into the workspace — `git clone` over `https` or `ssh` only, with the `git` found on `PATH`, never over a file `sync` writes, into the Forge or out of the workspace; when `init` asks for what the flags do not give, it lists the URLs first and asks, the default no. A clone is recorded nowhere, and `sync` never updates or removes it. `craftar repos` lists those repositories in an existing workspace — `present`, `missing` or `blocked`, with their URLs — and `craftar repos clone` clones the missing ones. With `--new-profile <name>` (optionally `--like <profile>`), `init` first writes one new file in a Forge directory, `profiles/<name>/profile.yaml` — the recipes and targets chosen, nothing else of the template — behind a git gate and never committed, then starts the workspace on it; in a terminal the profile list offers `0) a new profile`.
- F5 PM tool and internal platform per profile [working] (P1): in a Forge that declares `schema: 3` or above, a profile's `integrations` block selects recipes and gives params. `integrations.<slot>.kind: <kind>` selects the recipe named `<slot>-<kind>` — `integrations.pm.kind: azure-devops` selects `pm-azure-devops`, a recipe that lists, say, the MCP ingredient and a rule describing where stories live — and every scalar of the block is the param `integrations.<slot>.<key>`, cited in a body as `{{integrations.pm.org}}`. An integration with no `kind` gives params only. A schema 3 Forge is read only by craftar 0.27.0 and later; below `schema: 3` the block is ignored, without a warning; a `kind` with no recipe stops `sync`. In a Forge that declares `schema: 4`, an MCP server takes the params its ingredient declares, so one server serves every client: `url: "{{integrations.idp.url}}"`, with `integrations.idp.url` declared in the ingredient's `params`, renders each profile's own URL, and `.mcp.json` and `.kiro/settings/mcp.json` get the same rendered server. A declared key with no value stops `sync`; a key the ingredient does not declare is left as written, with a warning when some layer gives it a value; below `schema: 4` a server is written exactly as the Forge holds it. A schema 4 Forge is read only by craftar 0.28.0 and later. Tokens are referenced by `authEnv`, never stored (FM-8).
- F6 Local services per workspace [working] (P1): `craftar services up | down | status`. A `service` ingredient is a Docker Compose fragment plus the files it mounts. `sync` writes it under `.craftar/services/<name>/`, with the stack `.craftar/compose.yaml` — a Compose `include` of every fragment — for no target, text always LF without a BOM (a file listed as `binary` is copied as bytes), and records each file in `craftar.lock` (schema 3 only for a workspace that has a service). They are generated files like any other: `status`, `diff` and `sync --check` treat them the same. `craftar services up` reads the lock, not the Forge, and refuses to start a stack with a missing or hand-edited file, or with a stack or fragment the lock does not record; `down` stops it and `status` shows it. `sync` never runs Docker; `up` needs Docker Compose 2.20.0 or later. A Forge that holds a `service` ingredient is read only by craftar 0.25.0 and later.
- F7 Project templates [list | install working] (P1): `craftar templates list | install`. A profile's `templates` block lists packages per kind — `dotnet-new` today — with an optional `source` feed. `craftar templates list` shows what the profile declares; `craftar templates install` runs `dotnet new install` once per entry, into the user's own template store. Nothing installs implicitly — not `sync`, not `init`, not `doctor`. An entry of a kind this CLI cannot install (`npm-create`, `nx`) is listed, skipped and warned. A `source` carrying a user or a password is refused; authentication is NuGet's. Planned: a generated rule mapping archetype → template, and a wrapping `/create-project` command.
- F8 Drift and reverse contribution [working] (P2): `status` reports drift; never overwritten without `--overwrite-drift`. `craftar drift show` lists the hand-edited files, whether the Forge also changed each and whether the edit can be promoted — with a path, its diff; `craftar drift discard <path...>` is a `sync` that also regenerates the named hand-edited files (their edits are lost) and removes a named hand-edited file the Forge no longer produces; `craftar drift promote <path>` carries one hand edit of a `.claude/` file into the Forge's working tree — a value in the profile's `params` or `sections` when the edit is only that, otherwise a variant for the workspace's profile — gated on git and proved before the first write; it never syncs and never commits.
- F9 CI [--check working] (P2): `craftar sync --check`; `craftar diff --exit-code` gives the same verdict with the diff that explains it. `AGENTS.md` has a byte budget, `agents-md.maxBytes` (default 32768, Codex's `project_doc_max_bytes`; `0` turns it off): over it every plan warns, naming the largest rules, and when a recipe, the profile or the workspace sets it, `sync --check`, `status` and `diff --exit-code` with no path fail — a writing `sync` still writes. Planned: GitHub Action / Azure Pipelines task; pre-commit hook.
- F10 Registry and dashboard [working] (P2): a writing `sync` records its workspace in `~/.craftar/registry.json`; `craftar workspaces [--fetch]` prints each one — profile, stack, targets, Forge, last sync — with a status computed on the spot (`up to date`, `outdated`, `drift`, `no lock`, `missing` or `error`, plus `forge moved` when the Forge's commit is no longer the lock's), reading a remote Forge from the cache unless `--fetch` is given; `craftar workspaces forget <dir>` and `prune` remove entries; `CRAFTAR_NO_REGISTRY` turns the registry off, for CI runners and throwaway checkouts. From the Forge's side, `craftar forge impact` lists every registered workspace that reads it — by its path, by a git remote, or through another clone — with what its next `sync` would do; a workspace synced on CI, on another machine or with the registry off is not in it. `craftar ui [--port <n>]` serves these views as a local page in a browser: the table of `craftar workspaces` and, for a registered workspace, what `status`, `diff` and `explain` say about it and what `recipes` and `ingredients` say about its Forge. It is read-only — it writes nothing (the Forge cache is used as every reader uses it), reaches no network (a remote Forge is read from the cached copy, and the page says so) and never runs `sync`: it prints the command to copy. It listens on `127.0.0.1` only (port 4747 by default; `--port 0` takes a free one), answers `GET` only, and every answer that carries data needs a token generated for that run, carried in the address it prints — whoever holds that address can read what the reading commands print, so open it only in a browser of the same user on the same machine, exactly as printed. It takes no `--workspace`, and exits 1 when the registry is off or cannot be read. `craftar ls` stays the view of the recipes and ingredients resolved for one workspace.
- F11 Craftar as an MCP server [read-only working] (P1, P2): `craftar mcp [--workspace <dir>] [--fetch]` is a read-only MCP server the AI coder starts, over stdin and stdout — registered in its own MCP configuration, or for a whole team as an ordinary `mcp` ingredient that `sync` writes like any other server. It serves the one workspace it was started in through seven tools that only read — `status`, `diff`, `explain`, `recipes`, `ingredients`, `targets`, `doctor` — each answering with the data its command prints, so the agent can say "run `craftar sync`" instead of editing a generated file. It writes nothing — no workspace file, lock, registry or Forge (the Forge cache is used as every reader uses it) — reads no network unless started with `--fetch`, and never returns a hand-edited MCP configuration file; a result can carry the Forge's profile names, so register it only where that is acceptable. Upgrade every machine to craftar 0.29.0 or later before adding it to a shared Forge. Planned: writing tools (`sync`, `add recipe`); a Claude Code plugin and an Agent Plugin as thin shells over the CLI.
- F12 Diagnostics [working] (P2): `craftar doctor [--fetch] [--strict] [--json]` checks this machine — Node ≥ 22, `git`, `~/.craftar`, the registry, the Forge cache — and, inside a workspace, its configuration and Forge, the plan's warnings, declared parameters with no value (an `error` when a file the plan writes cites one, a `warn` when nothing does), the variables a written MCP server declares in `authEnv` or references as `${NAME}` and the environment lacks (names only, never values), the lock, `status` and registration, and — in a workspace with a local service — Docker with its Compose plugin and the variables a service fragment needs that nothing sets (names only), and — when the profile declares templates — the `templates` block and, for a `dotnet-new` entry, the .NET SDK — and the planned `AGENTS.md` against its byte budget; each finding is one line — `ok`, `warn` or `error` — with the command that fixes it; it only reports (nothing is written to a workspace, a lock or the registry) and reads a remote Forge from the cache unless `--fetch` is given; it exits 1 on an `error`, or on a `warn` under `--strict`; `--json` is a contract for tooling. Planned: a rulesync check once it is a dependency.

## Invariants (each derived from a failure mode; these are the constraints Craftar is built against — the one marked (planned) is a design commitment, not yet enforced by the code)

- Never touch a file not in the lockfile — unknown files are preserved; one at a path the Forge would write is reported as a collision (FM-1).
- Never hash raw bytes — normalize LF, UTF-8, strip BOM; compare JSON structurally. Claude Code and AGENTS.md outputs keep the EOL and BOM of the file they replace; Kiro output is always CRLF without BOM (FM-2).
- Never leave an orphan on disk — `--check` fails on it and `diff` shows it as the removal of the whole file (a hand-edited one as a header, since sync keeps it) (FM-3).
- Never require a manual mirror — everything a second target needs is generated (FM-4).
- Never split a rule from its reviewer — one ingredient, two outputs (FM-5) (planned; today the rule and its reviewer are separate ingredients (rule/<name>, agent/<name>-reviewer) grouped by a stack recipe).
- Never inline a volatile value — declared once in the profile, injected as params wherever cited (in a schema 4 Forge, inside an MCP server too); a parameter an ingredient declares with no default, that a file the plan writes cites and no layer sets, stops `sync`: nothing is written until it has a value (FM-6).
- Never translate — language is an attribute of the ingredient (FM-7).
- Never store a secret — an MCP ingredient declares `authEnv`, the environment variables its server needs, names only, never a value (an item shaped like a known token fails the load); with `claude-code`, `sync` writes `.claude/settings.craftar.example.json`, each declared name with an empty value, for the developer to copy into their own untracked `.claude/settings.json`; `craftar doctor` names the variables a written MCP server declares in `authEnv` or references as `${NAME}` and the environment lacks, never their values; `craftar import` refuses ingredients holding secret-like values, and a `forge:` URL holding credentials is refused; in a schema 4 Forge, a value rendered into an MCP server that is a URL with credentials or a token of a known format fails the plan, and the message names the field, never the value — a check, not a guarantee: a token of an unknown format still passes; a Forge file that is not valid YAML is reported by an error code and a position at most, never by quoting the line; one its schema refuses is reported by key, never by a value it holds (FM-8).

## Targets and capability coverage

`craftar targets` prints the capability matrix from the CLI's own table; `sync` decides from the same table which ingredients a target does not write, and a test fails when a cell and its emitter disagree. Nothing is dropped silently: an ingredient aimed at a target that cannot express it is skipped with a warning that names it; a fallback is planned. Three words: native — written in the tool's own place for that type, as the Forge holds it; converted — written in another form (frontmatter or a banner added, references rewritten, another container format, or folded into a shared file); unsupported — not written, sync warns and names the ingredient.

| ingredient type | claude-code | kiro | agents-md |
|---|---|---|---|
| rule | native (`.claude/rules/<name>.md`) | converted (`.kiro/steering/<name>.md`) | converted (`AGENTS.md`) |
| agent | native (`.claude/agents/<name>.md`) | converted (`.kiro/agents/<name>.json`) | unsupported |
| command | native (`.claude/commands/<name>.md`) | converted (`.kiro/steering/commands/<name>.md`) | unsupported |
| skill | native (`.claude/skills/<name>/<file>` or `.claude/skills/<name>.md`) | converted (`.kiro/skills/<name>/<file>`) | unsupported |
| mcp | native (`.mcp.json` and `.claude/settings.craftar.example.json`) | native (`.kiro/settings/mcp.json`) | unsupported |
| script | native (`.claude/scripts/<file>`) | unsupported | unsupported |
| steering | unsupported | native (`.kiro/steering/<name>.md`) | unsupported |
| hook | native (`.claude/hooks/<file>`) | unsupported | unsupported |
| service | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported |

`service` is aimed at no AI coder: `sync` writes it under `.craftar/` for no target. `craftar targets` also prints what each converted cell changes.

## Status

Phase 0 (done) — foundations: Forge schema; layer resolver with exclusive slots and params; `sync`, `diff`, `status`, `explain`, `ls`, lockfile, drift and orphans; `import --from claude-code`, reusing a base whose render matches when a second client joins the Forge; `forge variants`, `forge diff`, `forge unify` (base, variant, `take: param` or `take: section`); sections — client-specific blocks in ingredient bodies, overridden per profile and workspace, each client's content inferred by import or extracted from a variant by `forge unify`; emitters for Claude Code, Kiro and AGENTS.md; an oracle suite against a private hand-built workspace plus a synthetic suite in CI on Linux and Windows (byte-identical reproduction of a hand-built Claude Code + Kiro workspace; second sync is a no-op; Forge edits reach both targets; manual edits surface as drift and survive; removed ingredients disappear; unmanaged files untouched).

Phase 1 (in progress) — client profile. Shipped: the read-only catalogue — `recipes`, `ingredients` and `targets` with the capability matrix; a remote Forge — a git URL and `ref`, a per-machine cache (`craftar cache prune`), the schema 2 lock; the workspace registry and `craftar workspaces`; `add recipe` / `remove recipe`, editing the workspace's recipe choice; `craftar init` with flags; `craftar doctor`, what is off on the machine and in the workspace; `forge impact`, and `forge unify` planning the registered workspaces before and after, with `--prune-recipes`, and `forge promote`; an interactive `craftar init` — choose the Forge and the profile; `authEnv` on MCP ingredients — the environment variables a server needs, by name, and the generated `.claude/settings.craftar.example.json`; `craftar drift show` / `drift discard` / `drift promote`; a sync refused when a declared parameter has no value; `craftar import --report`, a Markdown report of an import; `craftar import --prefer-kiro`, a rule's source taken from its Kiro steering file; a profile's `integrations` block — PM tool and platform as recipes selected by the profile; `{{param}}` inside an MCP server; `craftar mcp`, a read-only MCP server — seven reading tools for an AI coder; `craftar ui`, a local, read-only dashboard of the registered workspaces, on `127.0.0.1` only; cloning a profile's repositories — `init --clone`, `craftar repos`; a new profile from `craftar init` — `--new-profile`, `--like`.

Phase 2 (in progress) — environment. Shipped: local services — `service` ingredients, `.craftar/`, `craftar services up | down | status`; `craftar templates list | install` — `dotnet new` project templates declared in a profile.

Later (not in a phase): a rulesync bridge for Codex/Kimi/Cursor specifics; `craftar docs validate`; a GitHub Action and an Azure Pipelines task around `sync --check`; writing tools for `craftar mcp` (`sync`, `add recipe`) and its Claude Code / Agent Plugin packaging.

Stack: TypeScript/Node CLI (commander, zod, yaml) with its own emitters for Claude Code, Kiro and AGENTS.md; rulesync planned as the conversion dependency for further formats. License: MIT. Open questions: Forge as separate repo vs monorepo; multiple Forges per workspace.

Trying it: install with `npm install -g craftar` (Node ≥ 22), or prefix any command with `npx`. Then, inside an existing Claude Code workspace, run `craftar import --from claude-code --forge <dir> --profile <name> --write-config` to obtain a Forge and a `craftar.yaml`, and `craftar diff` to see what a sync would change. Nothing in `.claude/` or `.kiro/` is rewritten until `sync`. Import a second workspace into the same Forge under another profile, and `craftar forge variants --forge <dir>` lists where the two differ. To start an empty workspace from a Forge instead, run `craftar init --forge <dir> --profile <name>`: it writes `craftar.yaml` and runs the first `sync` — or, in a terminal, run `craftar init` alone and answer its questions. When something fails, `craftar doctor` lists what is off on the machine and in the workspace, each finding with the command that fixes it.
